title: Apoptosis and Oncogenes
terms: Programmed cell death: DNA fragmented, cytoplasm blebs, contents NOT spilled into extracellular matrix (ECM), so no inflammation.
Bubble-like pieces the cytoplasm splits into during apoptosis, after DNA is catalytically fragmented.
Apoptotic cell contents are not spilled into the extracellular matrix, so no inflammatory response.
Normal apoptosis that shapes the body, e.g. formation of digits and neuron pruning.
Normal apoptosis removing damaged or diseased cells.
Normal apoptosis removing old cells, e.g. old liver cells.
Normal apoptosis removing excess cells, e.g. excessive CD8+ (cluster of differentiation 8) T cells.
Uncontrolled cell death from acute stress; cell ruptures, contents spill into ECM, inflammatory. 'Messy.'
Mitosis and apoptosis balanced; tissue size stays stable.
Mitosis outweighs apoptosis; new abnormal growth, e.g. cancers.
Apoptosis outweighs mitosis; tissue loss, e.g. Parkinson's disease.
Caspase 8 or 9; every apoptosis trigger activates one, which then activates the effector caspases.
Caspase 3, 6, 7; activated by initiator caspases; carry out apoptosis.
Cell fate (embryology), removal of survival factors, DNA damage, death signal, calcium (Ca2+) release; all converge on initiator caspases.
Initiator caspase of the INTERNAL (Bax/mitochondrial) pathway; activated from procaspase 9 by the apoptosome.
Initiator caspase of the EXTERNAL (Fas/FasL) pathway; activated from procaspase 8 by FADD.
Pro-apoptotic protein that OPENS mitochondrial membrane pores, releasing cytochrome C.
Mitochondrial protein released through Bax pores; combines with Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome.
Partner that combines with cytochrome C to form the apoptosome. OUTSIDE (confirm): apoptotic protease activating factor 1.
Cytochrome C + Apaf-1 complex; activates procaspase 9 into caspase 9.
Inactive precursor of caspase 9; activated by the apoptosome.
Anti-apoptotic protein that CLOSES mitochondrial pores, so no cytochrome C release; opposes Bax.
Survival signals that increase Bcl-2 transcription; their REMOVAL triggers the Bax pathway.
Listed: damage sensing (DNA damage via p53) and removal of trophic factors; figure also shows oxidative stress + calcium (Ca2+) overload at mitochondria.
More Bax → degeneration; balanced → homeostasis; more Bcl-2 → proliferation.
Membrane death receptor; activated by FasL, trimerizes, recruits FADD.
Ligand that binds Fas and triggers the external apoptosis pathway.
Fas-associated death domain (slide wording); recruited by trimerized Fas; activates procaspase 8.
Inactive precursor of caspase 8; activated by FADD.
Cytotoxic CD8+ T cell recognizes foreign antigen on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) and uses FasL to kill the cell.
During clonal expansion T cells show FasL but no Fas (no signal); old T cells express both Fas and FasL and kill each other.
Tumor cell expresses FasL; it binds Fas/FADD on the attacking cytotoxic CD8+ T cell, so the T cell undergoes apoptosis.
Mutated/overexpressed gene that can cause cancer.
Normal gene in apoptosis or cell cycle that mis-regulation or mutation could turn into an oncogene.
Gene for damage surveillance and negative cell cycle regulation.
Protooncogene GTPase; mutated Ras cannot hydrolyze guanosine triphosphate (GTP), so it stays active without growth signal.
Mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade downstream of Ras; activates Myc/Jun/Fos.
Transcription factors made constantly by mutated Ras signaling; push the cell repeatedly into the cell cycle.
Protooncogene kinase (protein kinase B) downstream of PI3-K; mutated AKT is constantly active → overproduces Bcl-2; figure: also blocks apoptosis and cell cycle arrest.
Upstream of AKT on figure: phosphoinositide 3-kinase converts PIP2 to PIP3; PDPK1 activates AKT (figure labels).
Tumor-suppressor; critical control component of cell cycle regulation. Mutated p53 cannot be phosphorylated → no p21.
Damage-sensing kinase that phosphorylates (activates) p53 on the figure.
Made by active p53; inhibits CDK (cyclin-dependent kinase) so the damaged cell cannot advance.
Retinoblastoma protein; binds and inactivates E2F. CDK phosphorylates Rb → E2F released.
Transcription factor for DNA replication genes; free E2F goes to nucleus and drives the cell cycle.
Tumor-suppressor; with Axin/GSK3 targets beta-catenin for destruction. Mutated APC cannot bind Axin/GSK3.
Partners APC binds to ubiquitinate beta-catenin. OUTSIDE (confirm): GSK3 = glycogen synthase kinase 3.
Wnt-pathway protein; high when APC is mutated → LEF/TCF transcription of cyclin D.
Wnt signaling stabilizes beta-catenin; beta-catenin acts with LEF/TCF transcription factors (figure labels).
Cell cycle regulator transcribed by beta-catenin; constant production pushes the cell through the cycle.
Oncogene delivered by a virus that causes tumorigenesis.
Viral Ras: mutated, constitutively active Ras; cannot hydrolyze GTP; signals through MAPK without growth signal.
Carries two viral oncogenes, E6 and E7; a significant cause of cervical and other cancers.
HPV protein that causes ubiquitination of p53 → proteasome degradation; cell loses damage control.
HPV protein that binds Rb so Rb cannot inhibit E2F; E2F pushes the cell into the cycle.
Normal epithelium → APC → Ras (adenoma) → p53 (carcinoma) → further mutations → metastasis.
Because cell cycle regulation is redundant, cancers rarely come from a single mutation; they build up multiple.
9-year-old dog: weight loss, diarrhea, anorexia, nodular colon masses, neoplastic cells on biopsy.
Variation in cell size / nucleus size; biopsy signs of neoplasia in the case.
traps: Bax OPENS mitochondrial pores (pro-apoptotic); Bcl-2 CLOSES them (anti-apoptotic). Don't flip them. (S10)
Internal (Bax) pathway → caspase 9; external (Fas/FasL) pathway → caspase 8. Both converge on effector caspases 3, 6, 7. (S8, S9, S12)
Initiator caspases = 8 or 9; effector caspases = 3, 6, 7. Initiator activates effector, never the reverse. (S8)
Cytochrome C + Apaf-1 = apoptosome. The apoptosome activates procaspase 9, not procaspase 8. (S10)
Trophic factors ↑ Bcl-2 (survival). Removal of trophic factors triggers Bax. DNA damage → p53 → ↑ Bax. (S9, S10)
More Bax → degeneration; more Bcl-2 → proliferation. Mitosis > apoptosis = neoplasia; apoptosis > mitosis = degeneration (Parkinson's). (S7, S11)
Protooncogene = NORMAL gene (Ras, AKT); oncogene = MUTATED version; tumor-suppressor = p53, APC. Ras and AKT are protooncogenes, NOT tumor suppressors. (S16–S24)
Mutated Ras cannot HYDROLYZE GTP (stuck ON). It is not 'cannot bind GTP'. Mutated p53 cannot be PHOSPHORYLATED. Mutated APC cannot BIND Axin/GSK3. (S18, S22, S24)
E6 → p53 (ubiquitination, degradation); E7 → Rb (binds, frees E2F). Easy pair to flip. (S29)
Colon cancer order: APC → Ras → p53 (adenoma after Ras, carcinoma after p53). Mnemonic: A-R-P, alphabetical. (S32)

know.title: Apoptosis vs necrosis
know.note: Direct comparison slide: 'Tidy and Cleaned Up' vs 'Messy and Inflammatory'.
rows: Cell rupture, contents spilled into ECM

know.title: Bax vs Bcl-2
know.note: Opposing pair that controls the internal pathway; ratio sets tissue outcome (S11).

know.title: Protooncogenes and tumor-suppressor genes
know.note: Classify each and know what the mutation does.
rows: Cannot hydrolyze GTP; active without growth signal
Constant MAPK → Myc/Jun/Fos → repeated cell cycle entry
Cannot be phosphorylated/activated; no response to ATM; no p21
CDK pushes cell through cycle despite damage
Cannot bind Axin/GSK3; cannot ubiquitinate beta-catenin
High beta-catenin → cyclin D → repeated cycling

know.title: Viral oncogenes
know.note: vRas copies a protooncogene; HPV E6/E7 knock out tumor suppressors.
rows: Mutated Ras; cannot hydrolyze GTP; constitutively active
Constant Myc/Jun/Fos → repeated cell cycle entry
Binds Rb so it cannot inhibit E2F

quiz.stem: A cell undergoes death in which its DNA is catalytically fragmented, the cytoplasm forms blebs, and no inflammation follows. Which process is this?
quiz.why: Fragmented DNA, blebbing, and no spilled contents (no inflammation) define apoptosis.

quiz.stem: Which example does the lecture give for the REGULATION role of normal apoptosis?
quiz.ok: Removal of excessive CD8+ T cells
bad: Removal of damaged or diseased cells
quiz.why: Regulation = excess CD8+ T cells; maintenance = old liver cells; surveillance = damaged cells; development = digits, neuron pruning.

quiz.stem: Which feature belongs to necrosis and NOT to apoptosis? (ECM = extracellular matrix)
quiz.ok: Cell contents spill into the ECM
bad: Cell is neatly packaged for removal
Cell death proceeds in a controlled way
quiz.why: Necrosis: uncontrolled, acute stress, rupture, contents spilled into ECM, inflammatory.

quiz.stem: A dog has progressive neuron loss in which apoptosis outweighs mitosis. How does the lecture classify this tissue state?
quiz.why: Apoptosis > mitosis = degeneration (e.g. Parkinson's); mitosis > apoptosis = neoplasia.

quiz.stem: Which caspases are the EFFECTOR caspases in this lecture?
After Bax opens mitochondrial membrane pores, what happens NEXT?
quiz.ok: Cytochrome C is released from mitochondria
bad: Bcl-2 transcription rises through p53 activation
FADD is recruited to the trimerized Fas
quiz.why: Bax pores → cytochrome C release → combines with Apaf-1 → apoptosome → procaspase 9.

quiz.stem: Which complex activates procaspase 9 in the internal pathway?
quiz.ok: Apoptosome of cytochrome C and Apaf-1
bad: Death complex of Fas, FasL, and FADD
Pore complex of Bax and mitochondria
Survival complex of Bcl-2 and trophic factors
quiz.why: Cytochrome C + Apaf-1 = apoptosome, which activates procaspase 9.

quiz.stem: A neuron is withdrawn from its trophic (survival) factors. Which outcome is expected from the slides?
bad: Fas trimerizes and recruits FADD protein
Necrosis follows with spilled ECM contents
quiz.why: Trophic factors drive Bcl-2; their removal is listed as a Bax pathway trigger.

quiz.stem: Per the S9 figure, which of the following can trigger the internal (Bax/mitochondrial) apoptosis pathway? (select all that apply)
bad: FasL binding to the Fas receptor
Increased Bcl-2 transcription by trophic factors
quiz.why: S9 lists damage sensing (DNA damage → p53 → Bax) and removal of trophic factors; the figure also shows oxidative stress + calcium (Ca2+) overload acting on mitochondria. FasL is the external pathway; Bcl-2 inhibits.

quiz.stem: In the external pathway, after Fas ligand (FasL) binds the Fas receptor and Fas trimerizes, what is recruited?
bad: Apaf-1 bound to released cytochrome C
quiz.why: FasL binds Fas → trimerizes → recruits FADD → procaspase 8 activated.

quiz.stem: A tumor evades cytotoxic cluster of differentiation 8 (CD8+) T cells by killing them on contact. Based on the Fas ligand (FasL) slide, what does the tumor express?
bad: Fas that binds the T-cell FasL
E7 that binds the T-cell Rb
quiz.why: Tumor anti-immunity: tumor cell expresses FasL, activating Fas/FADD on the T cell → T-cell apoptosis.

quiz.stem: A Ras mutation leaves the protein active WITHOUT a growth signal. What can the mutated Ras no longer do? (GTP = guanosine triphosphate; GDP = guanosine diphosphate)
quiz.why: Mutated Ras cannot hydrolyze GTP, so its off switch fails; it keeps signaling through MAPK.

quiz.stem: Mutated AKT promotes tumorigenesis mainly by which mechanism?
bad: Overproducing Bax to open mitochondrial pores
Freeing E2F by binding Rb protein
quiz.why: Constantly active AKT → high Bcl-2 → internal apoptosis inhibited → overpopulation.

quiz.stem: How does the lecture classify Ras, AKT, p53, and APC?
quiz.ok: Ras, AKT protooncogenes; p53, APC suppressors
bad: Ras, p53 protooncogenes; AKT, APC tumor suppressors
AKT, APC protooncogenes; Ras, p53 suppressors
Ras, APC protooncogenes; AKT, p53 suppressors
quiz.why: Ras and AKT = protooncogenes (S17, S19); p53 and APC = tumor-suppressor genes (S21, S23).

quiz.stem: A cell carries p53 that cannot be phosphorylated. After ATM (the damage-sensing kinase) senses DNA damage, what follows? (CDK = cyclin-dependent kinase)
quiz.ok: No p21, so CDK drives the cycle
bad: More p21, so CDK is inhibited
No E2F, so DNA replication stops
quiz.why: Mutated p53 can't respond to ATM → no p21 → no CDK inhibition → cell advances despite damage.

quiz.stem: Mutated APC (a tumor-suppressor gene) cannot bind Axin/GSK3. Which product is constantly transcribed as a result?
quiz.why: No APC–Axin/GSK3 binding → beta-catenin not ubiquitinated → high beta-catenin → cyclin D.

quiz.stem: Which human papilloma virus (HPV) protein inactivates its target by causing that target's ubiquitination and degradation?
quiz.why: E6 → p53 ubiquitination/degradation; E7 binds Rb, freeing E2F.

quiz.stem: A 9-year-old German Shepherd has nodular colon masses and neoplastic biopsy cells. Which mutation order fits the colon carcinoma slide?
quiz.why: Normal epithelium → APC → Ras (adenoma) → p53 (carcinoma) → further mutations → metastasis.

flags: S22 says 'No p21 means no inhibition of CDK1'; S21 figure (and S17, LC31) label it G1-CDK-Cyclin. OUTSIDE — confirm: G1/S CDKs are CDK2/4/6, CDK1 is the mitotic CDK. Use slide wording 'CDK' for now.
S10 step 3 reads 'inhbiting apoptosis' = inhibiting. No content change.
Checked against slide image: S23 figure shows 'β-Catenin'; S24 text writes 'Catenin B'. Same protein: beta-catenin. Spell it 'beta-catenin'.
Stop and Think has no slide answer (S30)
S30 asks whether mutated protooncogenes / tumor suppressor genes can be viral oncogenes; no answer on slides. Doc gives labeled reasoning from slide logic only. Confirm with transcript.
S7 calls mitosis > apoptosis 'Neoplasia (e.g. cancers)'; S11 calls the high-Bcl-2 state 'Proliferation'. Treat as the same direction; use each slide's own word in its context.
S13 expands FADD as 'Fas-associated death domain'. OUTSIDE — confirm: textbooks say 'Fas-associated protein with death domain'. Use slide wording.

S24 text says mutated APC 'cannot ubiquitinate Catenin B'. S23 figure shows beta-catenin phosphorylated (P) by the APC/Axin/GSK3 complex before the proteasome. OUTSIDE — confirm: textbooks say GSK3 phosphorylation tags it for ubiquitination. Use slide wording.
